Extending Our Knowledge on Network Governance
abs: The prevalence and importance of interorganizational networks for the delivery of public services has considerably increased in the last few decades. As Saz-Carranza states in his book, “Although they are inherently difficult to manage, interorganizational networks are popular organizing mechanisms” (p. 8). Networks are, however, not likely to replace classic bureaucracies but rather form an additional organizational layer that has far-reaching consequences for policy development and implementation, public service delivery as well as for the management of organizations themselves. The field of public management has responded to these changing empirical realities and we can observe an increasing stream of research on networks and collaboration in the public sector since the 1990s (see Isett et al. 2011 for a recent overview and discussion of different research streams). For a considerable time, however, the discussion had revolved around the questions, if, when, and how networks might be advantageous compared to markets or hierarchies. An important further step that also served as the point of departure for Saz-Carranza’s book was the conceptual article by Provan and Kenis (2008) on the governance of networks. In this article, Provan and Kenis explicitly depart from the discussion about networks as a form of governance and turn to the question what different types of networks we might be able to distinguish with regard to their governance, that is, from networks as a form of governance to the governance of networks. In that endeavor, they explicitly focus on networks as consciously created and goal-directed organizational entities. It is logical that talking about management and targeted governance of networks only makes sense in cases in which the networks are consciously created and in which goals exist at the network level. In their article, Provan and Kenis (2008) suggest three ideal types of network governance (they call them modes): the participant-governed, the lead organization-governed network, and the network administrative organization. In the latter case, a separate, neutral organization with several staff members or an individual person is installed to coordinate and monitor network activity, whereas in the other cases, all network members jointly govern the network or one of the organizations takes the lead. Provan and Kenis (2008) also introduced the idea that network governance is inherently characterized by fundamental tensions that cannot be resolved but only managed. They identify three tensions in this context: between efficiency and inclusiveness, between internal and external legitimacy, and between stability and flexibility. The study by Saz-Carranza builds on this research and combines it with insights from the research program on network management by Agranoff and McGuire. The book is an extended version of an article published by Saz-Carranza together with his PhD supervisor Sonia Ospina in JPART in 2011 (Saz-Carranza and Ospina 2011). Both are based on the author’s dissertation in 2008. The study presented in Uniting Diverse Organizations: Managing Goal-Oriented Advocacy Networks explicitly and exclusively focuses on networks with a network administrative organization (NAO). It examines four NAO-governed networks within the immigration policy domain in the United States from 2002 to 2006, “looking at how the NAO, a key actor, generates the conditions for joint action, despite lacking hierarchical authority over the network members” (p. 9). However, Saz-Carranza does not focus on the three tensions suggested by Provan and Kenis (2008) but introduces a fourth one, the tension between diversity and unity. Saz-Carranza argues that given the nature of goal-directed whole networks, this is the most crucial tension, which has to be managed. It is in these networks that organizations of different size, reputation, organization cultures, and goals come together to jointly achieve an outcome. Diversity, therefore, has on the one hand to be overcome in order to achieve network level goals but on the other hand has to be preserved, since the network is only sustainable, if the organizations continue to keep their individual characteristics. In this line of reasoning, networks will only be effective, if diversity can be positively used in generating resources and ideas for the achievement of network goals and the solution of joint problems. The tension between diversity and unity is of course not new and has been around in sociological thinking for over a century and figured prominently in the contingency theory in organization theory in the 1960s as the tension between differentiation and integration (which the author briefly acknowledges). The main contribution of the book is therefore not so much the conceptualization of the tension but how to manage it in public sector networks. However, the author could have linked the discussion on the diversity-unity tension more to the general discussion on differentiation and integration in various fields, which I will discuss in more detail in my critique below. The book gives a very brief introduction to the discussion on network governance and network management and positions the study within this body of literature. Chapter 2 presents an in-depth description of the networks (within case analysis) after a brief introduction to the US immigration policy domain. Network boundaries were based on membership lists. Data collection took place in two waves and consisted of individual, group, and phone interviews with a total of 31 interviews and included managers, NAO staff, and organizational members. All selected networks, that is, the executive director of the NAO were recognized in a National Leadership award program. Organizations or networks selected for the leadership award and therefore regarded by Saz-Carranza as “successful” cases had to show “that their leaders were tackling critical social problems with effective and systemic solutions, enacting leadership that is strategic, bringing different groups of people together, and sustaining results beyond any individual effort” (p. 30). In addition, they had to present documentation of results. A 50:1 nominee to awardee ratio according to Saz-Carranza signals a rigorous selection procedure and therefore can be seen as an indicator for the networks’ high performance (p. 30). The author acknowledges the selection bias that comes with the selection of cases out of this award program and the subsequent low variability. As a consequence, he focuses on “producing initial theory, using an interpretative logic, and cross-case comparisons along dimensions other than success” instead of making causal inferences about success factors (p. 109). Most of the organizations within the networks are nonprofit organizations whose mission is to promote immigrants’ rights. All networks carry out activities in three programmatic areas: community, civic, and technical education for immigrants; advocacy in favor of immigrants’ rights; and leadership development and organizing member organizations (p. 13). The most important achievements for all four networks (with various degrees of success) was the organization of mass rallies for immigration reform and immigrant rights that drew up to 500,000 people and achieved national media coverage. In addition, the networks managed to influence public opinion in their states and contribute to defeating anti-immigration policies. Chapters 3–6 present an extensive cross-case analysis and theoretical discussion of the study’s findings. The book ends with a summary conclusion of the findings and presents an extended appendix about the research design and methodology of the study. The author finds that “the successful networks studied here are simultaneously both united and diverse. The way these networks manage to avoid diversity undermining unity is by generating unity around three topics: A meta-goal, identity and the value of diversity” (p. 95). This means the management strategy has to focus very much on the cognitive aspects within the processes. Saz-Carranza identifies four activities by the NAO to manage the network’s paradoxical tensions: Activation (attracting and selecting members), facilitation (supporting member involvement, facilitating decision making), framing (common meaning making), and capacitating (help to increase the member’s and the network’s organizational capacities). Although these management activities relatively closely resemble the ones generally suggested by Agranoff and McGuire for public sector networks, especially activation and capacitating seem to be strongly influenced by the specific empirical context, US nonprofit networks in a controversial policy field. The author himself therefore limits the findings to networks with nonprofits and thus acknowledges this limitation. Even though the book does not go much beyond the 2011 JPART article (Saz-Carranza and Ospina 2001) with regard to the core findings of the study, I very much recommend it to students and scholars who would like to know more about but especially intend to study the management of networks. The book is very readable and does not resemble a “typical” dissertation manuscript that can sometimes be a bit lengthy. Instead, it is a very compact presentation of the study and its results with a short take away section for practitioners. The added value compared to the article is the in-depth description of the cases and detailed description of the research design and methodology (which we rarely read in journal articles these days, because of restricted space). The research design and methodology appendix might serve as a blueprint for similar studies in this area, which we need to make further progress in our understanding of the management of networks. I agree with the author that there is still a long way to go with respect to the management of networks rather than the management in networks (p. 95). I also agree with the future research themes noted in the discussion that need to be tackled, for example, individual competencies of people and organizations in the functioning of networks and a greater emphasis on time and processes. My points of critique revolve around three issues. First, as discussed above, the diversity-unity tension is basically a variation on the more general tension of differentiation and integration that all social systems face. Even though Saz-Carranza acknowledges the conceptual similarity, the book lacks a theoretical discussion that could have situated his arguments on the unity-diversity tension in public sector networks to the overarching differentiation-integration tension in sociology and organization theory. Second, tensions and their management are not new in the organizational theory literature. Saz-Carranza would have done well to discuss what is generally known about coping with organizational tensions. Third, the diversity concept as used in the book could be more refined. In the literature on teams for example, the question of how the diversity of teams affects their performance has been center stage for at least a decade. Because results of empirical research about the relationship between the two variables have been mixed, Harrison and Klein (2007) suggested that scholars have to distinguish different concepts within diversity, namely variety, separation, and disparity. Depending on the specific concept, the effect of diversity on performance is different as meanwhile also shown empirically. Although variety, for example different (disciplinary) backgrounds, is likely to have a positive effect on performance, separation (opposing worldviews) might not. Disparity (different reputations) might yet have a different effect. The diversity concepts used in the book, that is, the variability of network members with regard to organizational demographics and cultures, reputation, budgets, size, goals, etc., are lumped together in one unifying concept. If the claims within the team literature about the multidimensionality of the diversity concept are correct, I am wondering, to what extent managing diversity and unity with regard to different organizational competences (variety) works in the same way as balancing different organizational cultures (separation) or differences in size or reputation (disparity)? For example, to what extent does an NAO have to apply the same management activities when trying to manage size and resource differences compared to diversity with regard to policy goals or competencies of member organizations? Including these issues, however, would have definitely made the book longer, more complex, and less accessible for practitioners. Since not only the management of networks but also publishing research involves the management of tensions, I regard these points not as a disqualification of the book but rather as important challenges for further investigation.

t: Public Service Motivation and Employee Outcomes in the Egyptian Public Sector: Testing the Mediating Effect of Person-Organization Fit
abs: This article examines a process, namely person-organization (P-O) fit, through which public service motivation (PSM) affects work-related stress, quit intentions, and organizational citizenship behaviors (OCBs). Using a sample of 671 professionals in the Egyptian higher education and health sectors, a mediation model is outlined and tested empirically using structural equation modeling. Our results show that PSM positively affected P-O fit, which in turn had significant positive associations with OCBs and negative associations with work-related stress and quit intentions. Although P-O fit explained a high proportion of mediation in the relationship between PSM, stress, and quit intentions, it only explained a low proportion in the relationship between PSM and OCBs. In general, our findings suggest that if public managers are desirous of improving employee experience at work, then achieving congruence between employees’ and organizational values is important.

t: Teaching MPA Statistics Courses: A Review of Textbooks
abs: Many researchers, scholars, and teachers in public affairs, policy, and administration programs face the challenge of teaching statistics and data analysis to masters students. Our students require a certain level of training and savvy for consuming, criticizing, and conducting statistical analysis and require preparation for a variety of careers in the nonprofit, public, and private sectors. Future tasks may include appraising employee work activities, evaluating data analysis presented by interest groups and lobbyists, assessing program and policy outcomes, and designing their own research projects to assess program outcomes. What are the best methods for teaching Masters in Public Administration (MPA) students? Should instructors focus on teaching students to consume statistics or produce them? Should instructors rely on statistical programs to teach data analysis? And what text books will best support our efforts to prepare MPA students for the varied works lives ahead of them? Here, we present five book reviews that focus on nine textbooks used in MPA programs throughout the United States. The reviewers draw from their own experiences teaching MPA students to highlight the strengths and weaknesses of the books under review. This set of reviews offers an assessment of some of the textbooks available to instructors and ideas for how to best use them to teach MPA students. Reviewers were invited to select books they use, or have used, in the classroom in order to provide an insightful review for JPART readers. We hope these reviews will be useful to newly minted PhD’s prepping their first data analysis course as well as to more seasoned instructors looking to incorporate new materials in the classroom.

t: Information and Uncertainty in Policy Implementation: Evidence from the Implementation of EPA Waivers
abs: Agencies must simultaneously weigh technical information along with the political and distributive consequences of their decisions. In a study of the US Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA's) implementation of federal pesticide regulations, I show that the EPA accounts for both case and constituency factors. I assess the effects of both uncertainty and information in agency decisions. I offer the use of a multilevel model with three types of random effects to capture specific case factors (the crop, the pest, and the pesticide) to account for unobservable heterogeneity in outcomes. The models show that the impacts of uncertainty and information depend on the decision environment.

t: Teaching Statistics with Effective Textbooks
abs: I tried several textbooks for the Analytical Methods course that I teach before eventually selecting Berman and Wang’s Essential Statistics for Public Managers and Policy Analysts (2012) and Wang’s Performance Analysis for Public and Nonprofit Organizations (2010) for long-term use. In this review, I will discuss the challenges of teaching statistics to Masters in Public Administration (MPA) students, outline the features of these two books, and highlight how I used these books in my Analytical Methods course. For MPA programs, Analytical Methods (or Statistics) courses seek to train students, our future public managers, to competently apply statistical tools to accurately diagnose real-world problems and make sound decisions for the public interest. In an MPA program, Analytical Methods is probably one of, if not the most, challenging courses to teach. The selection of textbooks is critical in influencing students’ learning effectiveness. Based on my five years of experience teaching statistics to Masters level students in public administration and other fields, I have observed three major challenges confronting students in my classroom. First, some students, due to their lack of solid foundation in mathematics, are too overwhelmed by arithmetic formulas and hand calculations in textbooks to learn important statistical concepts and tools. These students may face a tough struggle in passing the course. Second, some students will understand formulas and calculations in a mathematical sense, but they are not able to competently apply statistical tools in a real-world managerial context. Consequently, they cannot master and retain the knowledge and skills required to apply these tools after they have completed the course. This indeed undermines the original intention of providing such courses. The final challenge facing students is that many software programs have been developed to undertake complicated calculations for data analysis, but these programs have a steep learning curve. Without a quick and easy guide to the software programs, students may not be able to take advantage of such current computing technology in statistics, which in turn reduces students’ motivation to apply statistical tools in their real-world settings. Both Essential Statistics (Berman and Wang 2012) and Performance Analysis (Wang 2010) are MPA student friendly statistics textbooks. First, both books minimize the presentation of arithmetic formulas and calculations, using simple language to explain essential statistical concepts and techniques. As Berman and Wang (2012) point out, “Conceptual understanding and application are central to statistics, not arithmetic and cumbersome calculations!” (p. 1). The reduction of arithmetic calculations in the books makes statistical concepts more accessible to MPA students, especially to those with minimal training in mathematics. Of course, it is unrealistic for a statistics book to exclude all arithmetic and calculations because they can effectively enhance students’ understanding of concepts and techniques. These books do a good job of reducing the mathematical approach, without losing it altogether. Second, both books emphasize the application of statistical tools in analyzing real-world problems. They provide numerous real-world examples and demonstrate how to conduct data-based research in a public administration setting. Although both texts do a nice job in bridging statistical concepts and the managerial reality, Performance Analysis concentrates on applications in performance analysis, and Essential Statistics covers a more broad range of examples. In addition, both books include friendly instruction of software programs for students. Performance Analysis teaches how to use Microsoft Excel for data analysis as “Excel has apparent advantages in accessibility, cost, and graphical presentation… Excel functions in data analysis are sufficient enough for performance analysis in most public and non-profit organizations” (p. XV). In each chapter, Wang provides very detailed step-by-step instruction on Excel operation, along with numerous tables, charts, and screenshots, to facilitate students’ learning. Essential Statistics teaches the application of both SPSS and Excel programs, with step-by-step instructions as well. In the workbook along with Essential Statistics, Berman and Wang spend two chapters demonstrating how to use Microsoft Excel and SPSS to perform different data analyses that are covered in the entire textbook. Berman and Wang’s Essential Statistics comes with a workbook and a CD-RUM of data sets. The text is written in a very brief and concise style, with 18 chapters covering topics from research design, descriptive statistics, and bivariate relationship analysis, to ordinary least squares (OLS) regression, logistic estimation, and time series analysis. Throughout the entire book, Berman and Wang (2012) use simple, concise, and straightforward language to make the statistical concepts and techniques easily understandable and readily applicable. To the best of my knowledge, Essential Statistics is the thinnest textbook among those with similar content for public administration students or alike. In each chapter of Essential Statistics, they highlight the important concepts and key points, whereas they lay out additional in-depth knowledge on the topic for further learning. Thus, instructors can flexibly select the material from the book, especially the first 14 chapters, to meet their particular teaching needs. The accompanying workbook with Essential Statistics is nicely crafted with four clusters of exercises in each chapter: Q & A, critical thinking, application exercise, and further reading. The Q & A draws key questions from the text and provides answers to students. In critical thinking, the open-ended questions may stimulate students’ thinking and deepen their insight and thus could be ideal material for class discussions or small group activities. The data-based exercises allow students to use data to apply the analytical techniques to answer real-world policy and management questions. Seven real data sets are particularly provided in a CD-RUM with Essential Statistics, in the formats of both Excel and SPSS. The last chapter of the workbook describes each of the data sets in terms of data background, collection approach, and summary of variables. These data sets have been used for data analysis in the chapters; thus, the provision of the data may allow students to imitate the analysis process with the use of software programs for the purpose to better grasp the analytical skills. With the data sets, instructors can demonstrate how to input and manage data in a software program. The data set can also assist instructors to develop homework assignments and exam questions. In my class, I require students to write an applied essay in which they utilize the analytical skills learned in class to address real-world problems, and I encourage students to use one of the data sets provided with Essential Statistics. Performance Analysis by Wang (2010) arranges topics by statistics and covers descriptive analysis, bivariate analysis, and OLS regression. The book demonstrates, with great detail, how performance information can be collected, described, analyzed, presented, and reported for the purpose of performance improvement. Compared with Essential Statistics, Wang’s Performance Analysis concentrates more on basic analysis techniques such as group mean comparison with t test and OLS regression. It does not include more advanced analytical tools such as factor analysis, logistic model, time series analysis, path analysis, and survival analysis, which are briefly introduced in Essential Statistics. Similar to Essential Statistics, one of the strengths of Performance Analysis is that it addresses real-world questions with focus on performance analysis. In particular, Performance Analysis incorporates a factual case study in each chapter, starting by presenting a performance management scenario and then explaining the statistical tools that can be applied. In sum, both Essential Statistics and Performance Analysis nicely combine essential statistical concepts with real-world application to explain the assumptions, purpose, and operation of data analysis in public administration. Furthermore, these two texts complement and supplement each other in terms of conceptual explanation, analytical tools, results interpretation, practical application, software use, and practical exercises. Therefore, I assign both Essential Statistics and Performance Analysis to my students. In my one-semester Masters level statistics course, three sections are covered: research design, descriptive analysis, and inferential analysis. I do not exactly follow the book content, but reorganize the book material to fit with my course design. In the section of research design, I concentrate on three topics: (1) research approaches with focus on quantitative versus qualitative research, and descriptive versus explanatory research; (2) basic concepts of quantitative research, including data set, observation, variable, value, measurement level, and measurement unit; (3) the measurement of an abstract concept, for example, performance; and (4) data collection and management. Therefore, I incorporate chapters 1 and 3–5 of Essential Statistics and chapters 1 and 2 of Performance Analysis. In Essential Statistics, chapter 3 introduces measurement levels and how to measure an abstract concept using conceptualization and operationalization approach. Chapter 4 is an extension and application of measuring abstract concepts with a focus on performance measurement. Here, performance is an abstract concept, and the logic model is an application of conceptualization and operationalization in performance measurement. Chapter 5 discusses data sources, sampling skills, and data input, which leads students to the practical application of software programs—Microsoft Excel and SPSS. Finally, I included chapter 1 to discuss the ethics of data analysis and research—the integrity of purpose, the integrity of the process of analysis and communication, and the integrity of dealing with human subjects. All the chapters above in Essential Statistics do a nice job in presenting some of the fundamental knowledge of research design and basic concepts with plain language. Chapter 1 especially adds a great value to the book as it explains the guiding principles in data collection and analysis. From the general point of view, students should understand the possible violations of the ethics so that they can take reasonable care to avoid any wrongdoing while they deal with data. For the MPA programs per se, which train the future public managers, integrity of any aspect should be emphasized because the public managers may influence a large amount of citizens through their data use. I keep acknowledging the ethics of data analysis to students throughout the semester. I do not include chapter 2 of Essential Statistics in the section of research design in my teaching because this chapter focuses on relationships of variables and development of hypothesis, which might be too early for students who just start the course. I would rather assign this chapter for students’ reading later when I teach inferential analysis. In Performance Analysis, the first two chapters primarily address two questions: what is performance analysis and what are the major steps in performance analysis? The information is helpful because it provides a real-world context of the application of analytical methods. Although data collection and measurement levels are covered in chapter 2, other basic concepts of quantitative research are missing in the early chapters in Performance Analysis. In my classroom, I add some more basic concepts in the section of research design such as data set, observation, variable, value, and measurement unit, which are not sufficiently described in Essential Statistics or Performance Analysis. Based on my teaching experience, students usually lack a clear idea about what a quantitative data set should look like at the start of the semester. For example, students are often confused with the term “observation” if it is not explicitly explained. Without fully understanding these basic concepts about data sets, students cannot successfully grasp analytical methods and perform data analysis. Therefore, in my teaching, when discussing research design, I supplement the textbooks with an introduction to quantitative data sets and data components and then apply these basic concepts throughout the semester. I also briefly introduce different forms of data sets, such as cross-sectional data, time series data, and panel data so that students can identify the changes of observations. I include three topics in the section of descriptive analysis: (1) frequency distribution for nominal and ordinal level variables; (2) central tendency and dispersion measures for interval level variables; and (3) reporting data source and descriptive analysis. Chapters 6, 7, and 9 of Essential Statistics and chapters 3, 5, 6, and 14 of Performance Analysis provide very helpful material on these topics. Essential Statistics categorizes descriptive statistics into central tendency and dispersion measures and covered in chapters 6 and 7, respectively, with frequency distribution being a dispersion statistic. In these two chapters, simple formulas and easy hand calculations are involved in generating the descriptive statistics; application of these statistics is also discussed. Chapter 9 is an extension of chapters 6 and 7 with a focus on the application of descriptive statistics in the real world and how to report descriptive analysis using appropriate presentations of charts. Although Berman and Wang put chapter 8, which introduces contingency table that is used to analyze the relationship between two categorical variables, in the descriptive statistics section, I would like to move it to the inferential analysis section, along with other bivariate relationship analysis techniques such as mean comparison with t test and correlation analysis. I think it might make sense to concentrate on summarizing single variables with different measurement levels in the section of descriptive analysis. In Performance Analysis, chapter 3 uses performance data to vividly illustrate the calculation of frequency distribution, mean, median, and mode and their application in performance management. Chapter 5 covers performance variation with focus on the concepts such as variance, standard deviation (SD), minimum, maximum, and standardized scores. Chapters 4 and 6 of Performance Analysis are not included in my teaching because these two chapters deal with time series data, which is beyond my course design. Chapter 14 is highly useful for public managers as it discusses how to write a report on performance analysis. The chapter covers six subtopics for writing the executive summary, the introduction, the theory and design, the data collection, the results, and the conclusions and recommendations. In each of these subtopics, Wang (2010) provides a list of do’s and don’ts, respectively, followed by an illustrative writing sample. In my class, I particularly demonstrate how to write the introduction, data collection, and results of descriptive analysis while supplementing the writing of research questions along with the introduction and the measurement of relevant variables along with the data collection. Because I introduce the reporting issue right after students have learned the descriptive statistics, I leave the topics of writing of inferential analysis results as well as conclusions and recommendations, which are also covered in chapter 14, to the end of the semester. Inferential analysis refers to the computing process of using sample data to estimate the population. Topics in this section may include (1) sampling distribution and the confidence intervals of population mean, (2) bivariate relationship analysis with hypothesis testing, (3) multivariate regression, and (4) reporting the results of inferential analysis. Chapters 2, 8, 10, and 12–15 in Essential Statistics and chapters 7 and 9–14 in Performance Analysis are covered in this section of my teaching. Essential Statistics introduces t distribution (or sampling distribution) and the confidence intervals along with SD and z scores in chapter 7 without clear definitions of the concepts, which may cause somewhat confusion to students. I would suggest explicitly differentiating two sets of concepts: SD, z distribution, and z score as one set versus standard error (SE), t distribution, and t score as another set. The former belongs to descriptive statistics and the later are inferential statistics as they involve the estimation from sample to the population. For example, a z score indicates the distance of an individual score from the mean, measured by the number of standard deviations. A t score estimates the deviation of sample mean from the population mean, measured by the number of SEs. Performance Analysis does a better job by using separate chapters (chapters 5 and 7, respectively) for the two sets of statistics and introduces SE along with the confidence intervals of population mean. However, Performance Analysis does not provide definitions clear enough to differentiate the inferential statistics from the descriptive statistics either. Another possible problem in chapter 7 of Performance Analysis is the calculation of the confidence intervals of population mean. Wang provides different formulas for the calculation: for a small sample size, the critical t is used to determine the range; but for a large sample size, the critical z score is used to determine the range. The logic behind is that as sample size increases, the t distribution will become similar to the z distribution. However, the different formulas might be too complicated for students to understand. I would suggest consistently using the same formula with critical t score for the calculation. Regarding bivariate relationship analysis, both texts clearly demonstrate the circumstances to use different techniques—including contingency table, mean comparison, and correlation—based on the measurement levels of variables (see chapters 8, 10, 12, and 13 in Essential Statistics and chapters 9 and 11–13 in Performance Analysis). Both texts provide step-by-step instructions on how to operate the analysis process with Excel or SPSS programs. The interpretation of the analysis results is also well elaborated in the chapters of each text. Nevertheless, one point that might be overlooked in the two texts is that relationship analysis (including bivariate relationship analysis) with sample data consists of two steps: (1) to detect the relationship in the sample and (2) to test the significance of the relationship in the population. For example, contingency table analysis can show how the two categorical variables are associated with each other in the sample. However, whether the relationship can hold in the population with much more observations is unknown until the hypothesis testing with the chi-square test is performed. Similarly, mean comparison between two groups can show how the groups are different in terms of the interval level variable within the sample. But the t test functioning as hypothesis testing can verify whether the difference found in the sample still exists in the population. Of course, hypothesis testing will not be necessary if population data are used for analysis. Another point that the textbooks do not mention, but I emphasize in my teaching, is that confidence intervals of population means can serve for hypothesis testing on group mean comparison to determine whether the difference between two groups is significant with a certain confidence. This addition may serve to greatly help students better master the material by understanding the connection between concepts and the distinction between descriptive statistics and inferential statistics. Both texts do great job in introducing simple and multivariate regression models (please see chapters 14–15 in Essential Statistics and chapter 10 in Performance Analysis). The software operation of regression, the interpretation of model fit, the explanation of coefficients, the significance of each relationship, and the assumption of OLS estimation are all clearly written with sufficient material. The only one issue that may cause misunderstanding is the inclusion of Pearson’s correlation analysis in the chapter of Simple Regression (chapter 14) in the text of Essential Statistics. I would like to relocate it as a separate chapter in the cluster of bivariate relationship analysis. In the meantime, I put more emphasis on the similarities and differences between Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r) and regression coefficient (b) in my teaching so that students can distinguish between the similar terms. Although both correlation coefficients and regression coefficients are applied to a linear relationship and both show the direction of the relationship, a correlation coefficient indicates the extent to which the observations lie closely or loosely around a straight line, whereas a regression coefficient (the slope) tells how much the dependent variable is expected to change as the independent variable increases by one measurement unit. Again this is an important distinction that the texts fail to make, but are important for MPA students to master. There are some additional chapters in Essential Statistics beyond my one-semester course design. In particular, chapters 16–18 briefly introduce some advanced modeling techniques, including logistic regression, time series analysis, path analysis, survival analysis, and factor analysis. t: Putting Big Data in Context
Statistics: Not Only How but Also Why and When
abs: The introductory course in statistics is perhaps unique among courses commonly taught in masters’ programs in public affairs (MPA) in the amount of debate it generates, not only about how it should be taught but also about what should be taught. The Royal Statistical Society and the American Statistical Association have both suggested that the training of statisticians should be fundamentally different from that of those whose main job is to be informed consumers and occasional producers of statistical analyses. In public affairs programs, we are not training statisticians. Our hope is to instill some statistical literacy by introducing our students to statistical thinking, concepts, and rudimentary skills. However, providing such an introduction poses a number of challenges. Our students have varied backgrounds, diverse levels of training in quantitative methods, and preconceived attitudes toward such courses. These attitudes range from abject fear to a fondness for all things mathematical. In addition, the goals for such courses also vary. We want to ensure that our students can judge data quality, have a basic understanding of the logic of a statistical argument rooted in the formal treatment of uncertainty, can interpret statistical analyses, and present the results of such analyses to an informed–though not necessarily numerate–audience. In brief, we want our students to be critical, perhaps even skeptical, consumers of statistical analyses. We might also want to provide them with a foundation on which they can build should they choose to become able producers of such analyses. This lack of agreement, regarding what to teach and how best to teach it, translates into a difficulty in identifying textbooks for data analysis and statistics courses in MPA programs. There are a number of statistics and data analysis textbooks written specifically for students in public affairs programs. However, the lack of dominance of one of such texts further attests to the lack of an agreement on what should be taught, although their indifferent quality could be another explanation for their lack of popularity. Although there may not be agreement regarding the content, there can be general agreement on the goals of such courses. The goals of MPA programs are not that different from those laid out in the Guidelines for Assessment and Instruction in Statistics Education: College Report (GAISE; American Statistical Association 2005). These goals bear repeating here because they provide the criteria for judging the books reviewed here. Students should believe and understand why Data beat anecdotes; Variability is natural, predictable, and quantifiable; Random sampling allows results of surveys and experiments to be extended to the population from which the sample was taken; Random assignment in comparative experiments allows cause-and-effect conclusions to be drawn; Association is not causation; Statistical significance does not necessarily imply practical importance, especially for studies with large sample sizes; and Finding no statistically significant difference or relationship does not necessarily mean there is no difference or no relationship in the population, especially for studies with small sample sizes. Students should recognize the following: Common sources of bias in surveys and experiments; How to determine the population to which the results of statistical inference can be extended, if any, based on how the data were collected; How to determine when a cause-and-effect inference can be drawn from an association based on how the data were collected (e.g., the design of the study); and That words such as “normal,” “random,” and “correlation” have specific meanings in statistics, which may differ from those in common usage. Students should understand the parts of the process through which statistics works to answer questions, namely, How to obtain or generate data; How to graph the data as a first step in analyzing data and how to know when that is enough to answer the question of interest; How to interpret numerical summaries and graphical displays of data—both to answer questions and to check conditions (to use statistical procedures correctly); How to make appropriate use of statistical inference; and How to communicate the results of a statistical analysis. Students should understand the basic ideas of statistical inference, including the following: The concept of a sampling distribution and how it applies to making statistical inferences based on samples of data (including the idea of standard error); The concept of statistical significance, including significance levels and p values; and The concept of confidence interval, including the interpretation of confidence level and margin of error. Finally, students should know How to interpret statistical results in context; How to critique news stories and journal articles that include statistical information, including identifying what is missing in the presentation and the flaws in the studies or methods used to generate the information; and When to call for help from a statistician. I do not think that any of us who teach statistics in public affairs programs would quibble with these goals. We do, however, argue vehemently regarding how these goals are to be attained. One of the debates pertains to the use of formulas and the level of computation by hand versus reliance on statistical packages. Some believe that hand computation helps students understand and perhaps develop a better understanding of the nature and logic of the concepts underlying the formulas. Others see little merit in learning formulas and would relegate all computation to computers. Statistics is not a branch of mathematics and therefore fluency in sophisticated mathematics is not essential for a basic understanding of statistical logic, concepts, and methods. Having said that, it is also important to add that basic numeracy is essential and some willingness to make sense of simple formulas can go a long way in helping grasp basic concepts. Statistical software with drop-down menus has almost removed the need to know any formulas or conduct any computation by hand. But computers are not there solely to take the drudgery out of computation. Although we use them mainly to do statistics, they can also be used to teach and learn statistics. Their power as an instructor’s aide is often underutilized. Carefully designed examples based on real data coupled with good statistical software can be an excellent teaching and learning device that allows students to work and learn at their own pace. There is, however, a caveat that must accompany the virtues of learning and exploration at one’s own pace. Self-paced learning can work extremely well with motivated students, perhaps not so much with students who are questioning the need to learn this material in the first place. The judicious use of formulas can advance conceptual understanding. For instance, for a student with knowledge of basic algebra and some facility with algebraic manipulation, the formula for the slope of a regression line, can go a long way in helping understand the role of the correlation coefficient and the relative variability in the two variables in making sense of the regression coefficient. There is value in knowing this formula to gain a broader understanding of regression analysis. In the same vein, many statistical formulas that serve only as computational devices exist; they have no intuitive appeal and do little to advance one’s conceptual understating of the underlying principles. I am less certain about the virtues of hand computation. I am too prone to making simple computational errors and that perhaps contributes to my ambivalence, although I can see how, for some, the actual process of computing the value of a statistic can help advance their understanding of the concept it signifies. Almost 35 years ago, two books, both titled Statistics were published, which in my opinion are exemplars of a sound introduction in statistics. They both captured, in fundamentally different ways, the spirit of the guidelines mentioned above. The first sentence of the preface to Statistics by Freedman, Pisani, and Purves (1978) states: We are going to tell you about some interesting problems which have been studied with the help of statistical methods, and show you how to use some of those methods yourself, explaining why the methods work and what to watch out for when other people use them. They succeeded. Through the minimal use of mathematical notation and abundant use of charts, tables, pictures, and humor, the book provides a rigorous but benign introduction to statistical inference and also does a credible job of discussing the design of experiments and sampling. Moore’s (1979) book Statistics: Concepts and Controversies took a different path that focused, as the subtitle suggests, on the conceptual underpinnings and the use and abuse of statistics. It was not a textbook in the classical sense in that its coverage of the materials was selective and focused more on why rather than how. I do not think that these two books have been surpassed since, including by their revised editions. Unfortunately, neither of them would work as a textbook in the public affairs program because they do not cover all the material we seem to want to discuss in our courses and they lack examples that illustrate the use of statistics in public affairs. A book that blends these two texts would be ideal for public affairs programs. Jessica Utts’ Seeing through Statistics captures the essential styles of these two books and goes one step further by providing numerous examples, drawn mainly from newspapers (that is, public affairs) to illustrate the correct use, abuse, and misuse of statistics in daily life. Thus, Seeing through Statistics is a true effort to help students see the world through statistics. A consequence of that approach is that it does not follow the standard format of an introductory textbook, which usually begins with univariate analysis, progressing though bivariate to multivariate analyses, with digressions into probability, sampling distributions, hypothesis testing, and linear models. Organization is not the only thing different about Seeing through Statistics. It emphasizes understanding rather than computation and some might find the book too verbose. Numerous aspects of this book are creative and instructive. Most chapters begin with a few “thought questions” designed to facilitate group discussions about statistics in everyday life. Most statistics texts attempt to teach how to conduct a specific statistical procedure. Jessica Utts seems to be more ambitious and would like to convey a sense of not only how but, perhaps more important, when and why. She is quite successful in getting people to think about why and, on occasion, manages to help the reader understand the rationale behind the use of a particular procedure. She achieves that by providing examples that are detailed and designed to motivate statistical analyses rather than serving solely to illustrate a narrow statistical concept. The book is organized in four parts: Part 1: Finding Data in Life; Part 2: Finding Life in Data; Part 3: Understanding Uncertainty in Life; and Part 4: Making Judgments from Surveys and Experiments. t: The Challenge of Statistics Education in Master of Public Administration Programs: A Review of Two Popular Textbooks
abs: Teaching statistics in a Master of Public Administration (MPA) program is a unique challenge. MPA graduates are trained to serve the public good, generally from within the public or nonprofit sectors, and become an active part of the networks that shape the design and direction of public programs. Individuals in these positions are frequently immersed in technical information and must have the skills and conceptual knowledge to deal seriously with that information. Understanding statistics is a core skill for individuals engaged in original research (e.g., a professional program evaluator) as well as individuals who make decisions based on the analysis of others (e.g., a manager making budgetary decisions based on quantitative performance indicators). For this reason, the teaching of statistics and research methods in general is an important part of an MPA curriculum. There is a general consensus that MPA programs need at least one course on statistics as part of their core curriculum. While the Network of Schools of Public Policy, Affairs, and Administration (NASPAA), the accrediting body for graduate programs in public affairs, does not explicitly require a course focused on statistics as a condition for accreditation, most (if not all) MPA programs include statistics as a prominent, if not dreaded, requirement in their core. The implementation of this requirement, however, varies greatly across programs. There are many ways of approaching the instruction of statistics, ranging from a traditional approach starting from mathematical foundations, to a more tools-based approach that provides students with a cursory knowledge of statistical tests and the conditions in which they should be applied, without any detailed mathematical understanding of how these tools work. It seems that an optimal approach lies somewhere in between these two extremes. This essay investigates the needs of MPA students when it comes to teaching statistics, through a review of two leading textbooks in the field: Berman and Wang’s (2012) Essential Statistics for Public Managers and Policy Analysts and Meier, Brudney, and Bohte’s (2010) Applied Statistics for Public and Nonprofit Administration. These books were identified as the top two most commonly listed required readings via online searches for syllabi for statistics courses taught in accredited MPA programs.1 I argue that the commonalities between these two books highlight characteristic approaches to statistics education in MPA programs. These approaches align well with NASPAA’s student learning standards for the accreditation of graduate programs in public affairs. The newer NASPAA (2009) accreditation standards require that the programs demonstrate, across their core curriculum, student learning outcomes within five “universal required competencies” (Standard 5.1). MPA statistics courses can make positive contributions to all of these competencies: 1. To participate in and contribute to the policy process. 2. To lead and manage in public governance. 3. To communicate and interact productively with a diverse and changing workforce and citizenry. 4. To analyze, synthesize, think critically, solve problems and make decisions. 5. To articulate and apply a public service perspective. The contributions made by both books, and their varied approaches to making these contributions, are considered in the context of the first four of these competencies.2 In examining similarities between the books, this essay seeks to identify a set of general design principles that could guide any statistics course in an MPA program. On the other hand, the differences between these textbooks highlight the various ways a given course may be designed to suit the particular needs of the students and programs, depending on preparation, focus, and mission. Ultimately, this review is intended to spur continued discussion regarding, first, the core skills and knowledge MPA graduates need to be informed and effective leaders in the public sector, and second, a set of best practices for teaching these skills in the classroom. Empirical data and analysis are important forms of currency in the policy process. This is due to the complex nature of many policy problems—assuming some degree of shared values regarding a problem, policy systems (and the public and nonprofit organizations embedded in these systems) must work toward a better understanding of the underlying causal drivers of the problem and the likely efficacy of different policy solutions (Henry 2009). At the same, many policy debates are value-laden, and in practice debates over empirical evidence often become a proxy for normative belief conflict (Sabatier and Jenkins-Smith 1993). In these situations, one must be aware of the potential misuse of statistical analysis—the so-called use of “advocacy science” to support normative policy positions. What are the implications of this potential misuse of technical information for teaching statistics in an MPA program? Many MPA graduates work in organizations that actively participate in the networks that shape policy decisions. Technical information is used in these networks to inform, but also to persuade. For this reason, MPA curricula must enable students to be informed, critical consumers of policy-relevant research, and should ideally introduce a healthy skepticism of research produced by others. In terms of theoretical underpinnings, this means that students need to learn enough research methods to critically evaluate the validity of empirical claims. Both of these textbooks begin with a focused discussion of conceptualization, measurement, and research design. This focus is appropriate for an MPA statistics course. In a more traditional course focusing on mathematical foundations, it is generally sufficient to set up a discussion of statistical tools with a statement along the lines of let x be a random variable and proceed from there directly to descriptive and inferential statistics. Such an approach is not enough for students entering public service, however. MPA graduates need statistical tools, but more importantly they need to know how research conditions allow for valid conclusions regarding the nature of problems, underlying causes, and the likely efficacy of interventions. Expertise in working with data is not a sufficient condition for being an effective participant in the policy process. Students require an understanding of how to conceptualize variables and set up (or assess) a data collection strategy that deals with likely threats to validity. Both Berman and Wang and Meier et al. provide a solid grounding in research design. The first three chapters of both books review the major modes of research in the public sector and discuss conceptualization, measurement, and research design. In these chapters, students learn to differentiate between independent and dependent variables, express hypotheses about relationships between variables, and understand criteria for establishing causality. Students are also exposed to essential research designs that may be used to demonstrate causal relationships. At the same time, these chapters also underscore the primary differences between the texts. Although Meier et al. build arguments from fundamental concepts, then lead into examples and practical applications, Berman and Wang focus on applications first and elaborate on core ideas as they become relevant to the applied skills. These differences are illustrated in the books’ varied treatment of research design. Meier et al. provide a thorough discussion of experimental designs and quasi-experimental designs and explain the steps involved in actually carrying out a classical experimental design. This will help students to understand the essential logic of experimentation and validity of inferences and add a solid conceptual foundation for understanding policy and program evaluation. Berman and Wang, on the other hand, present a discussion of research methods as a chapter focused explicitly on program evaluation. Berman and Wang’s approach is useful for MPA students, given that program evaluation is both a core skill in public administration and primarily concerned with research designs that effectively balance the need to deal with alternative explanations against the need for research designs that are feasible and useful for decision making. Berman and Wang’s short but coherent synopsis of the process of program evaluation should be a useful and engaging introduction for students who wonder why they should care about research design. In their treatment of research design, Meier et al. provide greater detail on conceptual underpinnings, whereas Berman and Wang provide a more applied, terse, and high-level discussion. These differences are also illustrated in the books’ discussion of requirements for demonstrating causality. Although Meier et al. outline four requirements (time order, covariation, nonspuriousness, and the existence of a causal theory), Berman and Wang outline only two: correlation and a causal theory, which they describe as a “plausible cause-and-effect argument” (p. 25). It is not particularly unusual to find different minimum standards across texts—in this case, it is likely that Berman and Wang’s intention is to present a less complex picture in the hopes that students will remember and apply the essentials (which is, of course, preferable to remembering and applying nothing at all). Interestingly, both books include causal theories in their list of necessary conditions for demonstrating causality. A text focused primarily on mathematical foundations might be inclined to leave this detail out. In fact, it is an important message for students of public administration who should be encouraged to think through the mechanisms through which variables influence change in one another. It is through an examination of these mechanisms that students discover policy hinges that might attenuate problems of interest. In program evaluation, for example, students learn far more about how to improve problems by clearly expressing and testing the theory on which a program is based rather than simply testing whether program inputs led to desired outcomes in a particular study context (Weiss 1972). The importance of theory—what it is, and what it potentially contributes to research in the public sector—is explained thoroughly in Meier et al., who also engage in a clear and useful discussion of the differences between theories and models. Students will benefit greatly from this book’s focus on the development of path diagrams and models of hypothesized relationships. Although Berman and Wang do not engage in much discussion of causal theories, they do provide a focused coverage of research ethics in working with human subjects. This is an important and often overlooked topic in research design and an especially important topic for MPA students who, in the course of their professional duties, are likely to have access to large amounts of sensitive information related to organizational activities and target populations. It is important for MPA students to be sensitized to the need to responsibly use data about people and bring this understanding and knowledge into the workplace. NASPAA’s competency to lead and manage in public governance underscores the need for MPA programs to train students to take on leadership roles in organizations that perform a diverse array of functions. Independent of one’s level of participation in the policy process, statistical training has practical applications to better understand and improve organizational operations. Effective managers rely on empirical data and rigorous analysis to do their jobs better. In my own teaching experience, there are generally a number of students with serious doubts about the importance of taking statistics as part of a core curriculum. Drawing on examples (both hypothetical and real world) that demonstrate the usefulness of this toolkit in managing an organization is vital to earning buy-in from even the most skeptical MPA students. Both Meier et al. and Berman and Wang provide clear motivation for readers on this front, by offering examples throughout the narrative as well as in the problem sets. This feature of both books is vital to training MPA students who are not only well versed in core statistical concepts but who understand the importance of these tools in carrying out “routine” management functions such as developing and visualizing sound measurements of employee performance. One particularly nice feature of the Meier et al. text is that it shows how core theoretical concepts provide a logic for management decisions. This is illustrated in Meier et al.’s treatment of probability. Probability theory is a fundamental part of inferential statistics, and it is not surprising that most statistics texts include at least one chapter on probability. At the same time, formal training in probability theory is not strictly necessary to understand and apply basic statistical tools (e.g., Berman and Wang do not provide a focused introduction of probability theory beyond an “in greater depth” box presented as part of the discussion on hypothesis testing) (chapter 10, p. 173). In Meier et al.’s presentation of probability theory, clear applications of basic concepts to making management decisions are immediately presented—for example, they demonstrate how one may apply the general rule of multiplication to draw conclusions about whether events of interest are related or independent (chapter 7, p. 128), and how students might apply the binomial probability distribution to quantify the likelihood that a particular organization engages in racial discrimination (chapter 9, p. 155). Meier et al. offer an elegant approach to prepare readers for a solid conceptual understanding of p values, confidence levels, and logical errors in inference—topics that are discussed in more detail in subsequent chapters on inferential statistics. NASPAA’s universal required core competencies emphasize the need for MPA programs to train students to effectively communicate with others. The increasing importance of technical information in policymaking suggests that, at a minimum, public administrators must learn to communicate about scientific and technical issues in order to be effective participants of the policy process. Public administrators need to know how to read analyses done by others, and at the same time be able to clearly and honestly communicate the results of their own analyses to policy makers, funders, partner organizations, and other stakeholders. Despite these demands, the effective communication of policy-relevant information is not easy and is a well-known problem that lies at the heart of research on the degree to which science actually influences policy decisions (McNie 2007), and how science can be more effectively used to inform decisions that manage emerging and highly uncertain risks (Mitchell et al. 2006). On the other hand, clearly communicating the results of quantitative analyses is rarely a centerpiece of statistics textbooks. Berman and Wang and Meier et al. devote substantial effort to illustrate how students may represent frequency distributions, boxplots, contingency tables, and other visual displays of quantitative information. The authors caution students to avoid deceptive representations, for example, by scaling axes to make relationships appear more intense. Berman and Wang are particularly thorough in their advice to students on constructing tables and graphics that help to effectively communicate results. In addition to visual displays of data and analysis, it is also important for students to learn how to effectively communicate uncertainty in statistical analysis. Uncertainty is omnipresent in conclusions from statistical tests, and results are often not as clear as decision makers would like them to be. From a student’s perspective, it is important to know how to communicate this uncertainty and its implications for decision making. Students must learn how to properly interpret p values and confidence levels and understand how the decision making context may influence the need to be conservative in these interpretations. Meier et al. do a particularly nice job on this front through their discussion of how different alpha levels might make sense in different situations—as they explain, “(a) police department… may be able to accept a .05 probability that one of its cars will be out of service. But the fire department may require a probability of only .0001 that a fire hose will fail to operate” (p. 197).
