t: Financing Suburbia: How Chicago Suburban Financial Managers Shape the Financial Health of Their Communities
abs: Public financial management, a subfield of public management, studies the raising, managing, optimizing, and leveraging of financial resources. Most scholars and practitioners recognize the import of financial resources in furthering the aims and goals of public management. However, this subfield of public management receives relatively scant attention in the pages of public administration (PA) journals and other academic PA research outlets (Kioko et al., 2011). This undoubtedly is unfortunate, given how the study of financial resource management is exceedingly salient from both practitioner and academic perspectives. With respect to the former, the global financial crisis underscored the importance of public financial management in ensuring that all levels of government manage their assets and liabilities in a prudent and sustainable fashion so as to ensure timely provision of public goods and services in both the short and the long term. Recent financial crises in Jefferson County, Alabama; Harrisburg, Pennsylvania; and Stockton, California, to name just a few, strongly evince this. Related to the latter, the study of the financial decision making by governments as made by elected officials and their managers offers much “grist for the mill” for traditional public management researchers in further exploring important strands of public management research such as contracting, network management, performance management, and bureaucratic politics.

t: Data Analysis for MPA Students
abs: Concise Managerial Statistics, authored by Alan H. Kvanli, Robert J. Pavur, and Kellie B. Keeling, is a comprehensive and intuitive textbook for teaching graduate students in a variety of disciplines the fundamental concepts of data analysis and statistical inference. Through extensive use of illustrations and examples, the authors emphasize the practical application of statistical concepts and analytical tools while giving proper attention to the underlying theoretical frameworks. Providing detailed instructions for all data analysis tools covered in the textbook in Excel, Minitab, and SPSS along with the authors’ own Excel macro add-in file is unique and especially useful aspects of this textbook. Adding the plethora of additional resources for both students and instructors that accompany this text make it a great choice—from among many available—for use in the classroom. I have personally used this textbook for several years to teach a required data analysis course for graduate students pursuing their master’s degree in public administration. Upon successful completion of this course, I expect my students to be able to (1) identify and propose questions of analysis that are pertinent to contemporary public policy and the broader study of public administration, (2) formulate a step-by-step approach for analyzing public management problems and policy questions, (3) identify the most appropriate methodological techniques for analysis of given research questions and available data, and (4) conduct data analyses using various methodologies covered in the course. Many of my students come from backgrounds without much emphasis on mathematical skills or statistical concepts, if at all. Although these students find the textbook challenging, the learning curve is not insurmountable. I attribute the approachability of this textbook to the authors’ ability to break down complex topics and explain them in everyday language while not ignoring the mathematical and theoretical foundations of the concepts being taught. I very much appreciate this approach and believe it contributes to a successful learning environment for my students; it certainly helps students accomplish the learning objectives I have laid out for the course. Although many of the textbook’s applied examples are topic specific to a business context, there are sufficiently relevant examples and appropriate practice exercises for students of public policy and/or administration. For example, I often create my own examples for use during class lecture, but always assign homework problems directly from the textbook. Practice exercises can be found throughout each chapter (not only at the very end of each) and are always categorized as problems to help students (1) understand the mechanics of the chapter’s section topic, (2) extend the topic and its use by applying new concepts, and (3) use computer data sets for further application of each statistical concept. The progression of difficulty, multitude of practice exercises, data sets and computer application problems, and detailed explanations of simulation exercises all offer ample opportunity for students to practice the tools and techniques covered throughout each chapter, which I believe is an essential component of developing statistical analysis skills. In Concise Managerial Statistics, chapters 1 through 3 cover the important fundamentals of data collection, presentation, and descriptive statistics. These chapters lay the foundation for the remainder of the textbook by introducing essential vocabulary, providing clear differentiation of data types and levels of measurement, describing various means of graphically displaying data, explaining frequency distributions, and covering the most commonly used measures for summarizing and describing data. The appendices to these chapters are especially useful as the authors walk students through each mouse click required to produce the graphs and statistics in Excel, Minitab, and SPSS. These instructions make it possible for even the first-time user of the software packages to professionally analyze and present data for a variety of purposes. Because our Masters in Public Administration (MPA) is a terminal degree program aimed at preparing students for professional careers in the public and nonprofit sectors, I exclusively use Excel for all statistical applications throughout the course. Although I agree that using Excel for data analysis is not always the most user friendly, and Excel does not have the power of other software for conducting statistics, I firmly believe having expertise in data manipulation, analysis, and presentation in Excel is most beneficial for my MPA students because it is what will be most widely available when they enter the workforce. In addition, feedbacks from several alumni of our MPA program have indicated that federal and state agencies often use the ability to generate pivot tables in Excel as an important metric for gauging expertise in the software and data analysis skills. Because the students entering my class are typically not proficient in Excel, the textbook’s focus on its use and detailed explanations are essential for my students to gain this necessary expertise. Chapters 4 thorough 6 focus on theoretical concepts of probability and probability distributions. These are the chapters that my students often find most challenging, yet I believe are essential for understanding the application of inferential statistics. In these chapters, the authors make use of contingency tables and Venn diagrams to introduce basic probability definitions and rules, as well as to provide relevant and understandable examples to explain the fundamentals of random variables and several discrete and continuous probably distributions. For this information, the authors’ extensive use of illustrations and summaries of formulas are especially helpful for students. Chapter 7 introduces the key concepts of sampling and statistical inference. Here, the authors use Excel to show students how the means from multiple samples can be described with the frequency distribution tools students learned in earlier chapters and then translated into a sampling distribution for calculating probabilities. The statistically empowering central limit theorem is also introduced in this chapter. I believe chapter 7 of this textbook is best described as a culmination of the prior six; this is the point each semester when my students begin to see the payoff of several weeks’ worth of struggling through learning unfamiliar concepts that seem vague and disparate. This chapter always seems to refocus and reinvigorate students as they begin to feel equipped to use data analysis to answer research questions that are relevant and interesting. The remainder of the textbook covers application of statistical tools for inferential data analysis. Chapters 8 and 9 introduce hypothesis testing and apply the concept to means testing a single and then two or more populations. Chapter 10 provides the tools necessary for analyzing categorical data. Chapters 11 and 12 cover correlation and both simple and multiple regression using ordinary least squares. Finally, chapter 13 introduces the basics of time series analysis and forecasting. In each of these chapters, the authors continue to provide appropriate, practical examples of application for each analytical tool covered, to explain each step for using Excel, Minitab, and SPSS for data analysis, to offer formula summaries and illustrations to aid students in learning, and to provide numerous opportunities for students to practice each new skill learned. In addition, the authors are particularly adept at walking students through each step of the process for hypothesis testing—taking time to show students how to state the null and alternative hypotheses, to identify the appropriate test statistic, to calculate the value of the test statistic, to predetermine an alpha level and testing procedure and then use these to make decisions about whether to reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis, and finally to offer a practical conclusion based on the results of hypothesis testing that addresses the initial research question. Focusing on each of these important steps and using repetition to reinforce proper procedure is an aspect of this textbook that I find highly commendable. This approach is one of the many reasons I find the textbook to be valuable for teaching data analysis to MPA students. Aside from the content of the textbook and useful aspects of content presentation I outlined above, the resources that accompany this book for both students and instructors are some of the best on the market. Particularly unique to this textbook is an Excel macro add-in file that was developed by the authors. As mentioned earlier, I teach the course exclusively in Excel format because it is the most widely available software in the workforce my students are entering into. I believe this approach gives my students more advanced Excel skills than the average MPA graduate, which makes them highly competitive on the job market and well qualified for their employment positions. In this textbook, the KPK Excel macro is a data analysis tool pack that further enhances the Excel expertise of my students due to its two advantages over Excel’s built-in data analysis add-in file. First, the KPK macro file offers some data analysis capabilities that Excel does not have. Second, for the data analysis tools that are replicated, the KPK macro file offers them in a user-friendlier format that is easier for students to use and interpret. The downside of this approach, is that the KPK macro file is not usable in versions of Excel for Mac, which is becoming increasingly popular among my graduate students. However, when Microsoft implemented its significant upgrade in 2007, the textbook authors wrote and issued an updated version of the KPK macro file so that it would remain compatible with Microsoft Excel. After personally e-mailing the textbook authors for the updated version, I was able to share the new file with my students and continue its use for my class. Student resources offered in addition to the textbook and Excel macro add-in file include a CD that offers extended content of each chapter along with the databases and data files (in Excel, Minitab, and SPSS formats) for all examples and exercises contained in the textbook. Resources for qualified instructors include an instructor’s manual, Powerpoint slides, and test bank questions for each chapter of the textbook. These are perhaps the most comprehensive resources accompanying any textbook I have used. Overall, I believe this book is an excellent resource for a beginning level graduate course on data analysis and statistics. Although the textbook is geared toward students in a business program, I find it relevant and useful for students in public administration as well. While I sometimes find it necessary to adapt the examples and applications of the book’s concepts toward a more public sector focus, the book’s contents are certainly within the realm of appropriateness for training our future public managers and leaders.

t: Local Government Management and Performance: A Review of Evidence
abs: Local governments play a critical role in delivering services to the public.Over recent decades scholars have begun to empirically examine the relationship between the management and performance of local governments, locating this in economic, contingency, and resource-based theoretical frameworks.In this study, we undertake a comprehensive assessment of what is currently known about the management-performance hypothesis in local governments by integrating the empirical research that has been published over the past 40 years.We uncover 86 empirical articles that rigorously test the management-performance hypothesis and apply the support score review technique to the findings of these studies.Our analysis suggests that scholars have yet to explore all of the approaches to local government management with the same vigor.The majority of attention has been focused on the concepts of organization size, strategy content, planning, staff quality, personnel stability, representative bureaucracy, and networking.The evidence points toward strong positive performance effects resulting from staff quality, personnel stability, and planning, and moderate support for the benefits of networking, representative bureaucracy, and strategy content.Subanalyses reveal different relationships across dimensions of performance and organizational levels within local governments, and that the British and American scholars that have dominated these studies have largely drawn upon divergent theoretical perspectives.Directions for future research are also considered.Local governments are responsible for the management and delivery of key public services in countries worldwide.From picking up the garbage and cleaning the streets, to the provision of schooling and care for the elderly and vulnerable, these organizations invariably lead the development and implementation of innovative solutions to new and pressing social problems.Local governments, in addition to being at the forefront of delivering and providing the public services on which citizens rely, are often also the most public face of the state.The "street-level bureaucrats" who deliver local public services play a vital role in shaping what it means to be a citizen through their interactions with clients and service users (Vinzant and Crothers 1998).The management and performance of local governments is thus an issue of both timely and enduring importance to researchers, policy-makers, and citizens alike (see Sharpe 1970).

t: Regulatory Democracy Reconsidered: The Policy Impact of Public Participation Requirements
abs: A broad range of procedural mechanisms designed to promote public involvement in regulatory decision making have been instituted at all levels of government. Depending upon the literature one consults, one could conclude that these procedures (1) enhance regulatory stringency by fostering access by previously underrepresented groups, (2) reduce regulatory stringency by institutionalizing access by regulated industries, (3) could either increase or decrease stringency depending on the relative strength of organized interests in the agency’s external environment, or (4) have no effect. This study investigates whether mechanisms designed to promote public involvement in administrative rulemaking affect the stringency of US state environmental regulation. The results suggest that requirements to provide public notice of agency rulemaking do not have a significant effect on the regulatory compliance costs imposed on industry, but mechanisms that provide direct access to rulemaking processes serve to decrease these costs. This effect is evident for access both to the agencies promulgating environmental regulations and to external entities reviewing these regulations. For promulgating agencies, the effect does not appear to be conditional on the relative power of societal interests. The results provide some evidence, however, that political officials respond to the strength of environmental and industry groups when reviewing agency regulations.

t: The Search for Credible Stories in the Public Sector
abs: Storytelling is everywhere. Politicians tell stories, public managers tell stories, street-level workers tell stories, citizens tell stories, the media tell stories. Yes, we all tell stories. So what? Well, that depends on the role that storytelling plays in our (working) lives. It is my assumption, and that of some of my colleagues in Public Administration and elsewhere in the social sciences, that storytelling can be a quite important aspect of one’s (working) life; at least in some lives some of the time and not necessarily in everybody’s life all of the time. Stories, to use John Forester’s (1993) phrase, do certain work. Through stories we order, we tell others what has happened (and might still be going on), and also what we find important (and what not), whom we trust (and whom not), and so on. Stories help to make sense and give meaning to events. And good stories, like good jokes and impressive numbers, are things people tend to remember. When told by good storytellers, stories can be quite persuasive. Stories emplot reality through the way they select, order, and describe events, actors, and a setting. A plot arises from the way story elements are brought together into a coherent unity. Stories answer questions like these: When did all the trouble start? How did it get so bad? Who was involved? To be sure, not everything is a story. If there are no events described, if there is no setting and if there are no actors, there is no story. In addition, storytelling can be an aspect of a certain practice, but that does not make the whole practice storytelling. There are for instance interesting narrative aspects to social science, but to look at social science as merely storytelling will not get you very far in understanding the practice. But stories can certainly do important kinds of work. Storytelling has been a topic in the study of Public Administration and Policy Making for quite some time. Although Martha Feldman, John Forester, Ralph Hummel, Thomas Kaplan, Emery Roe, Donald Schön, Deborah Stone, Dvora Yanow, Jay White, and others have talked about storytelling, it did not lead to many peer reviewed publications, unlike in Sociology and Organization Studies. Perhaps the size of the community is too small. Most probably the dominance of a methodological paradigm that has had little interest in storytelling has also played a role in excluding storytelling. The last decade has seen more activity in the realm of Narrative Public Administration (e.g., Sonia Ospina and Jennifer Dodge’s articles in Public Administration Review, the work of Mark Bevir and Rod Rhodes and various articles of Michael Jones, Greg Hampton, and Mark McBeth in policy analysis). More articles and books featuring storytelling have appeared in the previous decade than in the 1990s (probably more articles and books have been published in general, so that is just one kind of measurement). This essay looks at two of the most prominent books using storytelling that have been published in the last 10 years: Cops, Teachers, Counselors: Stories from the Front Lines of Public Service and Governing Fables: Learning from Public Sector Narratives. In the remainder of the essay I will focus not so much on the substantive topics of these books (front line work and public management), as on the question: how do these authors use stories and storytelling to investigate their particular topics? For the sake of clarity I will not use the noun “narrative.” It is used by the authors of the two books, but the meaning of the noun narrative differs. The authors do use the term story in the way I have described it above, and so I will stick to this term. A decade has passed since Cops, Teachers, Counselors was published. Still, the book has not received the attention it deserves when it comes to its use of stories. The book’s topic is street-level work and workers, post-Lipsky. Maynard-Moody and Musheno argue that times have changed. It is time to see that teachers, cops, counselors and others who represent the state in interactions with citizens/clients are not just bureaucrats but people who meet and judge others. The common focus had for a long period been on the way workers “apply the state’s laws, rules, and procedures to the cases they handle” (9). In contrast, the analysis of the stories these authors collected “reveals that workers are constantly attentive to who clients are, acting on their assessment of people’s character and identity.” (13) If Lipsky’s street-level bureaucrats were preoccupied with their own survival, the workers Maynard-Moody and Musheno met often told. . . stories about going the distance, even putting their careers at risk. Their stories do not reveal an intensive focus on their narrow self-interest or that of their agencies. Street-level workers tell of many cases or situations when they made their work harder, more unpleasant, more dangerous, and less officially successful to respond to the needs of the people in front of them (19). Typically, “the street-level workers first establish citizen-clients’ identities and then respond” (154). And, as the authors conclude, “[m]ore than bureaucratic politics, identity politics shape the citizen-clients’ outcomes” (153). Maynard-Moody and Musheno build their argument mostly on the stories generated throughout a 3-year period of fieldwork. Stories, they explain, use events to create plotlines that lead listeners from a beginning through a middle part towards an end. Stories “create miniature worlds” (26) that we can enter. They simultaneously “bring institutions to life” (29) and present the storyteller’s “cognitive maps” (25). And they are both a microscope that can be used to examine minute details of a practice and a telescope to look at general themes and patterns. In frontline work, stories serve as “cultural artifacts that hold, in compact form, the norms, beliefs, and decision rules that guide actions and choices” (30). In the end, then, “to tell a story is to tell a moral” (31). Storytelling occurs in all social settings, but it is not easy to record stories in situ. That is why this research team used interviews in order to access workers’ stories. Nevertheless, as the authors argue, interview stories are still more natural than regular interview answers, because they have a life outside of the research process. While telling a story, the storyteller might even be reliving the events recounted. To tap into ongoing concerns, the interviewees were asked—in preparation for the interviews—to make notes on stories they lived through or heard about. In total, the research generated a set of 157 stories from 48 street-level workers in five sites. As indicated above, Maynard-Moody and Musheno did not have naive ideas about the content of these stories. They knew that stories are “not photographically accurate” (26). Moreover, the street-level workers clearly “told only certain stories, in part because workers have an image of their work and imagine what others want to hear about it” (29). What the authors call good research stories are those that report in a rather detailed way on what happened, showing the listeners how events were experienced and showing the complexity of street-level work. Such stories are “often ambiguous and multilayered: they reference both rules and morality to defend decisions, reveal internalized as well as interactive conflict, and document shifting positions over time” (25). Asking for stories, and making room for them, thus led Maynard-Moody and Musheno to rich data. Other data were also generated through regular interviewing, document study, survey, observations—data that seem to serve most of all to contextualize. The Appendix of the book says more about its strategies and methods. The analysis of the stories entailed various rounds of reading, coding, and discussing among the research team. This procedure helped to establish the themes that are discussed in the second and third part of the book: identities and moralities. A rather straightforward qualitative data analysis, so it seems. But the content of the stories surprised the authors. The absence of stories about problems of fitting cases with laws, rules, and procedures helped them to come to a crucial finding: street-level workers are as much or even more focused on the people they meet than on matching cases with rules. More information on this aspect can be found in Maynard-Moody and Musheno’s (2013) contribution to the excellent volume on interpretive research. Also interesting is the use of stories in the book itself. The authors decided to keep the stories intact, because coded phrases would lose too much meaning when they were “disembodied” from a story (177). That is why 36 full stories are spread throughout the book. Although it is not very clear how the stories that ended up in the book were exactly chosen, the authors indicate their preference for those stories that are detailed enough to bring the reader closer to the world of street-level workers. We could also assume that the analysis led to a certain set of themes that became the chapters of the book. The authors selected a couple of good stories on each theme. The selected stories do not just put the street-level workers in a different light, highlighting workers’ focus on citizen/client identity, but in the spotlight. Indeed, the stories help to bring the storytellers, their agency, and their moral judgment into view. The workers are given voices, and the workers speak to the reader through these stories. Of course, the stories in the book are still recorded, transcribed, and edited interactions between interviewer and interviewee, but that is the kind of data the research produced. Maynard-Moody and Musheno’s third chapter—Story Worlds, Narratives, and Research—is one of the best introductions to narrative research I have come across. The authors tell us what we need to know about stories and narrative research in the mode they have chosen. The chapter contains both an enthusiasm for stories and an awareness of their limitations. A clear risk of basing research on stories is that we might not hear much of the regular and the routine. The authors themselves admit this. They write that stories are “biased towards the memorable, the nonroutine and the dramatic,” that they “exaggerate the good, the bad, and the unexpected and downplay the everyday.” (32) My own research on policing (van Hulst 2013) confirms that it is hard to access mundane frontline work through storytelling in interviewing, because it does not seem tellable enough to the interviewees. That is to say, why would workers tell you about their really mundane encounters? If a police officer went to a call about a sheep that wandered to the wrong side of a ditch, her colleagues will probably not find it worth hearing about. Would the officer then tell a researcher about it? Not really. This is also the case with telling about events for which workers feel embarrassment. Still, such stories tell us interesting things about the work of street-level workers. Although many of the cases in Maynard-Moody and Musheno’s book get to the heart of what the job is about for those who do it, hearing a lot of stories that seem hardly worth telling would help us to identify even better the way procedures, systems, morality, setting, clients, and workers interact. It would probably require long-term observation to get at the mundane and the embarrassing. In the end, however, asking for stories gets the interviewer beyond generalities or espoused values that they might hear if they did not ask about specific episodes in the lives of informants. Storytelling is also closer to the everyday conversation of street-level workers than responding to interview questions or survey questions. In addition, we might argue that asking for stories and presenting them “uncut” is a humane way of generating and dealing with data. In fact, it parallels the way street-level workers themselves often operate when they think a client/citizen is worthy. They offer this client/citizen the space and time to tell their story, resisting the rush to interpretation. Academics, politicians, and public managers alike, often fond of summaries and tables that tell them exactly what they seem to need to know, are well advised to read Maynard-Moody and Musheno’s stories, to think them through, to digest them. In Sandford Borins’ Governing Fabels: Learning from Public Sector Management on the other hand, the author himself is the most prominent storyteller. Borins’ book is the product of a special project. It has its origin in courses on narrative and management that the author taught over the preceding two decades. To Borins, storytelling denotes “a distinctive means of ordering experience; a particular mode of perceiving, representing, and communicating events; a way of structuring meaning in time” (xi). According to Borins, there is a lot of storytelling in practice: “Consider the contemporary public sector and its range of actors. . . Now consider the innumerable stories these actors generate, communicate, and enact” (2). As a consequence, “skill at engaging with, creating, and communicating compelling stories must be considered essential for both politicians and public servants” (3). Borins calls such skill narrative competence. The storytellers in Borins’ book are not politicians or public servants, however. His narrative data do not consist of interviews, speeches, or minutes of meetings, but of movies, television series, novels, memoirs, documentaries, and a scholarly book. Such data—whether fiction, nonfiction or a mix—abound and are easy to access. These are the materials Borins had been using in his classroom for years. Borins wants public management scholars to take the narrative turn. In this book, however, he does not lead us to the highway(s) of recent narrative analysis. He takes us down another road to the literary and film scholars who call themselves narratologists. t: Performance Information, Blame Avoidance, and Politicians' Attitudes to Spending and Reform: Evidence from an Experiment
abs: Performance information has been argued to assist politicians in decision making on budgeting and reform, but research on how political decision makers respond to performance information is sparse. Building on blame-avoidance theory, we develop novel hypotheses concerning the impact of performance information on politicians’ attitudes to spending and reform. To isolate the causal effect of performance information, we conducted a randomized survey experiment among 844 Danish city councilors. Information treatments showing high and low performance had a positive effect on attitudes to spending, whereas information on average performance had a negative effect on spending attitudes. Moreover, information showing high performance rendered politicians less willing to pursue reform. We discuss the implications of these findings for the role of performance information in public administration.

Measuring Agency Attributes with Attitudes Across Time: A Method and Examples Using Large-Scale Federal Surveys
abs: Public management researchers are interested in many characteristics of organizations that cannot be directly captured, making aggregated attitudes from surveys an attractive proxy. Yet difficulties in measuring meaningful attributes over time and across organizations have frequently limited statistical designs to a single organization or time. We offer a method for creating such statistical measures across agencies and time using item response theory. Focusing our attention on US federal administrative agencies, we marshal a variety of questions from surveys commissioned by the Office of Personnel Management and Merit Systems Protection Board and employ statistical models to measure three important attributes—autonomy, job satisfaction, and intrinsic motivation—for 71 agencies between 1998–2010. Our study provides a wealth of data for quantitative public management research designs as well as an adaptable framework for measuring a wide range of concepts.

t: Combining Structure, Governance, and Context: A Configurational Approach to Network Effectiveness
abs: This study explores the way in which network structure (network integration), network context (resource munificence and stability), and network governance mode relate to network effectiveness. The model by Provan and Milward (Provan, Keith G., and H. Brinton Milward. 1995. A preliminary theory of interorganizational network effectiveness: A comparative study of four community mental health systems. Administrative Science Quarterly 40 (1):1–33) on the effectiveness of designed and goal-directed interorganizational networks is extended and tested on the basis of 39 crime prevention networks (Safety Houses) in the Netherlands. Ten cases were subjected to in-depth analysis through documentation reviews, interviews, observations, and a survey among network participants. In the other 29 cases semistructured interviews were conducted with the network managers. The data for all 39 cases were analyzed with crisp-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis. The results revealed two different configurations for network effectiveness. Effective networks are centrally integrated networks that have been in existence for at least 3 years (age) and which show a high degree of stability. In addition, they either have considerable resources at their disposal or they have been set up with a network administrative organization. The results confirm core insights from Provan and Milward’s earlier study but also show that administrative resources can serve as a substitute for financial resources (and vice versa). The article concludes with suggestions for the further development of a configurational theory of network effectiveness.

t: Organizational Reputation, the Content of Public Allegations, and Regulatory Communication
abs: How does the content of public allegations impact regulatory communication strategies? Employing a multinomial logistic regression analysis and an original data set, this article analyzes the Israeli banking regulator’s nuanced responses to public expressions of opinion between 1996 and 2012. We demonstrate this agency’s greater propensity to acknowledge problems, yet mostly shift blame to others when faced with claims that regulation is overly lenient, and to deny allegations that regulation is excessive. These findings, although based on one institution, are important because they demonstrate an agency’s differential response to external allegations, given their content and its assessment of the relative threat to its reputation. They also suggest that external audiences may be able to shape agency attention and response by carefully framing their claims in light of their understandings of agencies’ distinct reputational vulnerabilities.

t: Mind the Gap: Dimensions and Influence of Street-Level Divergence
Focusing on Collaboration Techniques
abs: Students and practitioners have been focused on collaboration for some time as they study and move toward improving public administration and public policy outcomes. Agranoff’s (2012) Collaborating to Manage: A Primer for the Public Sector, Margerum’s (2011) Beyond Consensus: Improving Collaborative Planning and Management, and Williams’ (2012) Collaboration in Public Policy and Practice: Perspectives on Boundary Spanners bring together useful multiple issues involved when using collaboration approaches as tools to improve public policy and organizational performance. These three texts are reviewed as one focus area on collaboration. The focus of these is on the permeable boundaries of public and nonprofit policy areas through cross-functional efforts, cross boundaries of entities, and multiorganizational settings. Although each book has its own perspective on collaboration, this review discusses them separately, illustrating some common themes and distinctions. In Collaboration to Manage: A Primer for the Public Sector, Agranoff states that his book is “geared to professionals who work within and with the new, externally as well as internally geared bureaucracy – the ‘conductive’ public agency—and for students who are pursuing or will pursue careers on one or the other side of public programs in the network era” (p. ix). However, he also states that “this book is neither a complete manual nor a complete academic study of any one of the topics brought together to explain collaboration . . .” (p. 19). The bases of Agranoff’s eight core chapters are expressions of six delivered lectures and three conference papers presented between 2008 and 2010 at various universities. Agranoff cites many short interesting examples throughout the chapters, focusing on local, state, and federal government agencies, as well as nonprofit organizations. Agranoff’s insights are sharply on one theme developed throughout the text—that of collaboration, noting that “at one time collaboration referred to the cross-functional effort of persons working within agencies, it now also refers to those who cross the boundaries of organized entities working in dyadic, triadic, or networked relationships that are transactional in nature” (p. 2). The book focuses on six thematic issues of note: (1) contemporary conductive nature of organizations that serve the public, (2) the tools of interaction that need to be understood for their relational nature—such as regulations, contracting, fees, and vouchers, (3) how networks and other transactions are managed differently from traditional organizations, (4) the shared power of networks, (5) the need for intergovernmental management—both vertically and horizontally, and (6) the changing nature of traditional public organizations to ones that work collaboratively outside themselves. Chapter 2 contains information on the numerous methods of collaboration with both the public and the organizations that serve the public. These include informal practices and links, government tools, and formal public-nongovernmental organizations (NGOs). The issue of vertical and horizontal activity comes into play, with vertical efforts placed into action by interlocal collaboration and the horizontal action due to state or federal action. As such, different approaches are needed by managers to operate in these environments. However, a major focus is found in chapter 3 on the “conductive” public agency, which the author defines as “one that organizes itself to work ‘outside’ the agency as well as inside it” (p. 17) because “with open boundaries (it) can position itself for collaboration” (p. 17). He discusses how traditional bureaucratic organizations have evolved to become flatter and more open ones. In the past, public employees were typecast as enforcers of inflexible rules and procedures who aimed to protect the agency at the boundaries from nonconforming ideas and attacks. It was exactly as the old attitudinal saying “my way or the highway,” with no room for deviation. (I know as I used to be one of them in a former life.) Agranoff nevertheless points out that “a new overlay has been placed on the standard bureaucracy” (p. 53) to help it work better with outside agents and other government and program entities. The author illustrates a hypothetical conductive agency (figure 3.1, p. 57) as well as some typical agency examples to demonstrate this new focus. Agranoff then follows this with chapters that cover, in greater detail, issues that build upon these initial forays into collaboration management, discussing external agreements (chap. 4), managing agency connections (chap. 5), and processing deep collaboration through networks (chap. 6). In chapter 7, Agranoff details important efforts of identifying and overcoming barriers to collaboration and the avoidance of what he properly labels “collaboration failure” (p. 161). This concept is well covered, along with the types of collaborative power used to develop outcomes. This is a useful discussion to alert readers to the challenges they can face in undertaking this effort. In chapter 8, Agranoff focuses on what he calls the New Public Organization. This New Public Organization is one that “must operate in a sphere of governance, working together with other entities in contractual and forms of collaborative relation to seek the kind of public value expected of them” (p. 186). This moves organizations into a role of coproduction. Further descriptions of this new public organization are discussed throughout the remaining part of this chapter principally by using the Metro High School in Columbus, Ohio, as a model. The digital age is then highlighted as a new frontier for collaboration. Agranoff closes the chapter on the new public organization with the statement “I have tried to capture how this seemingly confusion is ‘organized’ – or at least might be organized” (p. 209). He then links collaboration to the New Public Management (NPM), a method of reform used in a number of countries (e.g., United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, Ireland, and the Netherlands). NPM applies private sector techniques to the public sector and is principally outcome based. The citizen is therefore the consumer. As a result, the key focus is on the private firms and NGOs. Accordingly, the resulting privatization, deregulation, competition, and partnerships all need collaboration efforts to be successful. The final chapter ends with 12 ideas the reader should take away from the collaboration literature—from polydiffusion to “collaborarchy” and points between. I had hoped to see more on boundary spanning and the role of individuals performing this task. Although Agranoff does touch upon this technique, it was cursory and not done to much depth. Numerous interesting charts, tables, and appendixes are found throughout the book, along with 16 pages of useful references. In addition, each chapter contains interesting small cases that trigger various approaches of collaboration. However, the index, although spanning more than 11 pages, is somewhat limited in the way the categories listed are laid out, making it difficult to find various key topics of interest in the text. The book Collaborating to Manage: A Primer for the Public Sector examines both theory and practice in collaborative public management and provides a solid basis to dig deeper into this interesting topic. In contrast, Beyond Consensus: Improving Collaborative Planning and Management by Richard Margerum looks at collaboration as a “concept that problems – whether defined by physical, political, socioeconomic, or other boundaries – need to be managed holistically” (p. 6). In his focus, stakeholders take center stage through a deliberative process, requiring consensus to reach final results. However, Margerum feels that full collaboration is really going beyond consensus, into implementation and evaluation. Building on his viewpoints, his focus is on what he calls the “seven Cs” to help explain collaboration. Briefly, these seven are as follows: (1) collaboration itself—used as a specific approach to planning and management, (2) communication—the sharing of information, (3) consultation—more formal process taken with stakeholders, (4) conflict resolution—ranges of processes, from formal to informal, used to resolve differences, (5) consensus building—steps taken to reach mutual agreement, (6) cooperation—independent work toward the agreed-upon goal, and (7) coordination—when all work together to reach the agreed-upon end state. This is an interesting way to link these dynamic principles together with the focus on collaboration. Margerum divides his book into four parts: (I) an Introduction that leans heavily on describing typologies of collaboratives, (II) a section that focuses on the consensus building process, (III) a section that covers the implementation of strategies into action, and (IV) a synthesis of all elements into practice and pathways into the future. In turn, his aim of the book is “to improve collaboration efforts and make them more effective in translating their work into success on the ground” (p. 17). To accomplish this, Margerum seeks to provide a theoretical basis for collaboratives and concrete indicators to use to assess collaboratives. Margerum successfully uses typologies to explain collaboration. Found nestled in chapter 2 and then expanded upon in part III of the book, these typologies help define how collaboratives operate and obtain results. Margerum lists the operational differences among collaboratives (table 2.2, p. 31) and states that “to influence a broader set of decision makers” (p. 33) than core stakeholders, he uses a typology of networks that can help make the collaboratives successful. As such, these typologies use the concepts of social, interorganizational, and political networks and are highlighted in the numerous interesting case studies he includes in the text. Thus, chapter 2 becomes a key focus area for readers to analyze and build upon. One of the collaborations cited by the author is very familiar to this reviewer from a former life in the federal government. The example of the International Joint Commission (IJC), which cuts across two countries, eight States, and two Provinces all to manage the Great Lakes’ waters, involves a key government agency in both Canada and the United States. Those readers with an interest in public participation will no doubt want to focus on chapter 4, wherein Margerum “drills down” on some key topics such as sample measures of facilitation, conflict management, and the assessment of public involvement, all useful tools. Margerum cites a concern among all those who perform collaboration as the need to assure that timely implementation occurs following expended efforts. He goes into some excellent detail on how implementation of this can be achieved through the use of various evaluation criteria, including procedural validity, underlying theory of the plan, and high-quality information, as he highlights the need for “well crafted goal and objectives” (p. 126). The principal title of the book “Beyond Consensus” comes into play in part III of the text through the author’s discussion of leadership, governance, and organization change, with a large spotlight on the role of boards. In addition, chapter 6 illustrates how collaboration is greater than conflict resolution or advising groups because collaboration is ongoing and continuous throughout the entire process. The author moves into chapters 7, 8, and 9 to pursue “the relationships between . . . sustained collaboratives and the social, interorganizational, and political networks that help collaboratives achieve results” (p. 179). As such, Margerum shows useful approaches for assessing strategies in each of these areas apart from discussing barriers to success. In addition, and just as important, is the author’s discussion of what happens when collaboration comes to an end. Margerum is quite honest in mentioning the “costs” involved in networks—from support funding needed, to shared power and decision rules for coordination. The topics of transparency and accountability are given little attention. Nevertheless, to his credit, Margerum includes excellent examples covering all of the key program measurement categories. In summation, Margerum states that “this book explains a range of different approaches that fit under the name of collaboration, and in particular how these forms translate consensus into results” (p. 250). As a conclusion to his approach, he highlights four types of approaches to obtaining results: 1. Passive—collaboration as an information and exchange process 2. Informal—social networking among those participating 3. Cooperation—collaboration seen as a plan or agreement 4. Adaptive network—needing ongoing adjustment and fine-tuning. A highlight of this book is Margerum’s perspective based on his many years of work in collaboration in the fields of natural resources, social services, land use, and transportation planning. He presents more than 40 case studies from the United States and Australia. In addition, the appendix includes a rich 15-page summary of his research methods and 10 pages of useful chapter notes. He concludes by discussing the future and trending of collaboration, including separate interesting questions for practitioners and researchers. Linkage among the various collaboration concepts discussed throughout the book must occur in order to make improvements—and just not provide feedback, as Margerum states “if these results are not forthcoming, a collaborative approach may not be the best way to address these problems” (p. 287). In Collaboration in Public Policy and Practice: Perspectives on Boundary Spanners, Williams takes an entirely different approach to the topic of collaboration, focusing on the role of those who facilitate collaboration—boundary spanners. In this book, Williams draws from more than 20 years of public sector management and consulting experience in health, social care, and community strategies. In doing so, he presents a behind-the-scenes look at collaboration through boundary spanning strategies and collaboration in the United Kingdom. The usefulness of his work is that his views appear to be quite easily translatable to other public policy arenas and countries because the process used is transparent. Williams defines collaboration as a “complex notion that attracts different interpretations and emphasis, and can be conceived as a means to an end or an end to itself – a set of principles to guide the conduct of public governance and management, or a project that is ultimately manifested in new forms and structures” (p. 15). Williams presents a brief discussion of other definitions of collaboration but then quickly moves to his topic of primary interest, boundary spanning. Boundary spanning is a growing concept in public administration and policy. Boundary spanners use techniques “that meander and weave across different types of boundary . . . these cut across the conventional boundaries of organisation, profession, sector and policy” (p. 31). Many readers will agree that “better coordination and integration of public services (is needed) to reduce duplication, to make better use of scarce resources, to meet gaps in service . . . and to promote citizen-centered and client-focused service delivery models” (p. 30). Better coordination requires people and organizations to collaborate to solve community issues, making boundary spanners critical in three areas: 1. Periphery of the organization—with actors looking out and others looking in through its walls 2. Overlaps between agencies—using personal relationships to continue coordination 3. In new spaces between agencies—creating unique structures and relationships. Williams notes that “boundary spanners” are one of two types: (1) individual actors who have a dedicated position and job to operate within multiorganizational settings and whose duties are completely devoted to boundary spanning activities and (2) a larger cohort of people who increasingly undertake boundary spanning activities as part of mainstream public management. Boundary spanners can be found at all levels of organizations—at the very top with leaders down through the ranks to the frontline, as practitioners delivering public services, commonly called street-level bureaucrats. Similar to Agranoff and Margerum, Williams mentions that the “blurring of boundaries” (p. 12) makes the need for collaboration and boundary spanners more critical to policy implementation. This is especially true in cross-sector issues. In chapter 4, Williams shares some interesting insights about the roles of boundary spanners and their key competencies. These roles are boundary spanners as (a) reticulists with the trait of being skilled in serving as “a bridge, a conduit, a filter and a gatekeeper” (p. 39), (b) interpreter/communicator, (c) coordinator, and (d) as entrepreneur. Several key tables are included that provide useful information on the types of collaborative experiences and competencies needed for the various types of boundary spanners to be successful. Williams even provides a sample job description for a boundary spanner in chapter 8 as he discusses implications for policy and practice. To portray a balanced view, Williams cites possible tensions and challenges that face boundary spanners as they undertake their work, including blurred professional relationships and the dilemma of multiple accountabilities. For those interested in leadership, Williams devotes nearly a chapter on the challenges for leaders who engage in boundary spanning. He uses that as a departure point for collaboration leadership. At the end of the book, the author voices concern over the absence of a professional group that would promote and accredit boundary spanning as well as the lack of clearly identified training for boundary spanners. He does, however, provide some clear ideas to better develop boundary spanners. In his concluding chapter, Williams laments that “remarkably, there is a general lack of research evidence on the effectiveness of boundary spanning roles, strategies and interventions, particularly in the public sector” (p. 152). As a result, there is a continuing need to focus more heavily on successful case studies and action research. A very useful element of this book is that there is a review of main points following each chapter as well as a variety of discussion questions that can easily be used in the classroom. The topic of boundary spanning is well covered, making this book useful for students. In addition, this thin but well-crafted text is crammed with 17 pages of references, making it more appealing to students and junior researchers than those undertaking more sophisticated research. The best way to compare these three solid books, all of which focus on collaboration, is in the form of their usefulness to various audiences. Agranoff’s book in many ways belongs in the public management student’s backpack due to its focus on public sector activities. On balance, Margerum’s book, even though it is a bit lengthy and “thick,” is a target text for both advanced classroom use and practitioners focusing on applications toward environmental and transportation planning. Williams’ text can easily be used in both the undergraduate and the graduate classrooms because the topic of boundary spanning is focused on those who are actively involved in this action. As a result, Williams’ book is best suited to students and practitioners who need to understand what it takes to “close the deal.”

t: Organizational History and Budgetary Punctuation
abs: The basic dynamics of punctuated policy change have been found to be present in a wide variety of political institutions from a range of countries. The presence—even commonality— of punctuated change has been clearly and persuasively demonstrated. A key challenge in the literature is now to identify the conditions and institutional arrangements that make punctuated change more likely. This article investigates the role of organizational history in punctuated budgetary change. An error-accumulation model of punctuation suggested by the institutional friction framework contends that budgetary punctuation results from a built-up need for budgetary change that had been prevented by slow-moving institutions. The need builds up until the institutions give way in the form of a budgetary punctuation. This explanation suggests that the probability of a punctuation in a given year is negatively related to having experienced such a punctuation in previous years. An alternative model—which we will call the institutional model—contends that the propensity for budgetary punctuation is endemic to specific organizations. These organizations possess inherent characteristics that predispose them to punctuated change. The institutional model suggests that the probability of a punctuation occurring in a given year is positively related to the organization having experienced such a punctuation in previous years. The article uses data from Texas public school districts during an 18-year period to test these competing models of policy punctuation. The results indicate that recent punctuated changes raise the probability of additional punctuated changes, supporting the institutional hypothesis.

t: Searching for Resilience
abs: Wildavsky’s Searching for Safety introduced the term resilience to public administration in 1988. Societies, he argued, face risks every day and increasingly do so as social and technical systems become more intertwined and interdependent. Wildavsky called for an investment, not just in prevention but in resilience. Societies, in his view, should focus on mitigating and absorbing shocks as well as prevention, which is often more costly and less effective as measured by cost-benefit analyses. Wildavsky, however, studied human error and the breakdown of technical systems as problems, as opposed to the types of terrorist acts that would later shape many US foreign and domestic policies. During the 1990s, the United States experienced a period of capacity building across all phases of emergency management; mitigation, preparedness, response, and recovery (Rubin 2012). The 9/11 terrorist attacks shifted emphasis and resources to prevention and protection. Never again, Americans vowed. The shift to prevention and protection, however, came at the expense of an all-hazards approach that promoted resilience from multiple hazards (Flynn 2007). Public organizations neglected more common and predictable disasters, both natural and technical, such as hurricanes and the collapse of critical infrastructures. The subsequent failure of initiative that characterized federal, state, and local response to Hurricane Katrina in 2005 led to a resurgence across the fields of public administration and political science in examining the determinants that lead to more resilient societies. With research remaining inchoate, we still search for resilience today, both in theory and in practice. Unresolved points of debate include: The very definition of resilience: Is it solely a reactive capacity for recovery or a more comprehensive set of outputs and outcomes that characterize safe, proactive societies? Scale of action: What is the appropriate scale of action or combination thereof (individual, organization, community, or society) to achieve successful results? At what level should we invest time and effort to increase resilience? Operationalization of resilience: What measures accurately operationalize the concept? Factors that facilitate and/or impede: What roles do external aid, competent governance, smart regulatory policies, tightly-connected communities, and the effective interface between decision makers and technical data-generating system, for example, play in promoting resilience? Two recent (and excellent) books illuminate and explore the concept of resilience and address these questions. In Building Resilience, Daniel P. Aldrich, who experienced the ill-effects of Hurricane Katrina and translated that experience into a powerful research agenda, studies the role that social capital plays in both facilitating and impeding disaster recovery. In their edited volume, Designing Resilience, Louise K. Comfort, Arjen Boin, and Chris C. Demchak take a sociotechnical approach, laying out a set of themes that characterize a broad definition of resilience. For full disclosure, I was Professor Comfort’s student at the University of Pittsburgh. In that role, I witnessed the development of Designing Resilience as well as the vision and intent of the authors. Both books explore multiple hazards and examine numerous cases with a mixed, though quite different, set of methodologies and theoretical frameworks. They both begin by addressing the elusive question: What is resilience? This essay is entitled “Searching for Resilience” as homage to Wildavsky, but also as an acknowledgment of our inchoate understanding of resilience in public administration and political science. Relatively little work has attempted to build a comprehensive definition that accurately depicts its complexity—which is Comfort’s and her colleagues’ contribution to the field, applying a sociotechnical, complex adaptive system approach. Aldrich takes a different tact, focusing on a narrower definition of resilience and operationalizing it at the neighborhood level. Both books explore a complex set of antecedents that facilitate resilience and multiple definitions of resilience that improve upon the traditional, engineering-bound, notion of bouncing back, as both acknowledge that change will and does indeed occur. Comfort and her colleagues define resilience as both a proactive and reactive process. To them, resilience is the product of a collection of decisions intended to reduce risk. They relate resilience to each phase of the disaster management cycle and argue that a resilient society is one that recognizes risk and effectively reduces that risk in the face of uncertainty prior to and/or during an extreme event. “Resilience is the capacity of a social system (e.g., an organization, city, or society) to proactively adapt to and recover from disturbances that are perceived within the system to fall outside the range of normal and expected disturbances” (p. 9). Resilience, according to Comfort and her colleagues, is not simply what people do or how they respond after an incident; it is cumulative and represents the intersection between several systems (social, technical, natural, and geophysical) as well as scales of action (individual, organization, community, and society). Aldrich takes a more traditional approach, operationalizing resilience, both quantitatively and qualitatively, through recovery-related variables (e.g., the rate of return for displaced persons, access to housing and other forms of assistance, and immigration rates). Aldrich skillfully explores variation in the rate of recovery across multiple cases at the neighborhood scale of action. In that way, Aldrich defines resilience by emphasizing how communities react to an extreme event: “Resilience is a neighborhood’s capacity to weather crises such as disasters and engage in effective and efficient recovery through coordinated efforts in cooperative activities” (p. 7). Aldrich’s intent was not to take a comprehensive position on where resilience begins and ends. However, others have couched resilience solely in the recovery phase as well (see Vale and Campanella 2005). This position diverges sharply from the viewpoint of Comfort and her colleagues and highlights the debate regarding timescale and whether resilience encompasses other phases (e.g., prevention, protection, mitigation, preparedness, and response). The following questions of timescale, defining resilience, and high-reliability models, explored by Comfort and her colleagues, deserve more attention from the field. For time scale, when does resilience as a phenomenon take place, only after an extreme event or during other phases and cooperative activities? When defining resilience, we can ask: Are communities that prevent and or mitigate hazards not resilient? By several definitions, resilience is solely the ability to recover from large-scale incidents; however, if an organization, community, or society recognizes risk and prevents a routine emergency from escalating or cascading into a large-scale disaster, are they, too, not resilient? And third, for high-reliability models, if resilience is not all-encompassing with respect to risk reduction, are organizations and societies that reduce risk simply safe or highly reliable (see La Porte 1996)? A comprehensive model (or set of models) for resilience like the one Comfort and her colleagues build provides a vision for an ideal set of outputs and outcomes that inform policymakers, emergency managers, and others concerned with risk reduction the world over. It is certainly ambitious and deserves further attention from the field. Although the books differ on timescale, common ground exists on the importance of collective action. Both books acknowledge the necessity of collective action to address shared problems, albeit focusing on different scales of action. Large-scale hazards rarely adhere to political borders. Countries and their political subdivisions often share substantial risk and the resulting asymmetry between risk, vulnerability, and public jurisdictions creates the impetus for collective action. Aldrich focuses on cooperation at the neighborhood level and how bonding, bridging, and linking social capital facilitate recovery. Comfort and her colleagues explore a separate set of interorganizational and international linkages. These concepts, social capital and cognition, offer two powerful and seldom studied factors that influence the rate of resilience. Various arguments have been made regarding the antecedents of resilience. Researchers focusing on recovery have explored factors such as the intensity of an incident, the amount of aid that enters an area, the performance of top public officials, pre-event social and economic conditions, and the role of pre-event regulatory regimes. Aldrich argues that in the long term, those factors take a backseat to social capital (or the social connections and structures that enable the flow of information and resources) in facilitating recovery. He suggests that existing levels of social capital (bonding, bridging, and linking) drive recovery and account for the variation between success and failure. Aldrich, for example, begins his book by describing how an immigrant community—a community lacking wealth and traditional forms of political influence within the City of New Orleans—leveraged their shared resources and willingness to work together to recover faster and more effectively than many other communities ravaged by Hurricane Katrina. Aldrich makes the argument that social capital produces negative externalities as well as positive results, arguing, in particular, that bonding social capital has been used to isolate groups by race, class, and ethnicity. He demonstrates how caste divisions rewarded in-groups and obstructed out-groups, drawing on evidence from the Indian state of Tamil Nadu following the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. Aldrich also notes historical research on Tokyo following the 1923 earthquake, which identifies seemingly systematic murder and harassment of minorities such as Koreans following the incident. Thankfully, Aldrich does not rely on metaphor or anecdote like many researchers who study social capital. He employs rigorous mixed methodologies across several cases. The book deserves praise. His broad definition of social capital, however, creates similar boundary challenges that Comfort and her colleagues experience with their comprehensive model of resilience. Specifically, at what point do researchers differentiate social capital from larger and more established sociological phenomena such as xenophobia, racism, caste systems in India, and the divisions between poor and more affluent communities? At what point do we just call those phenomena by their established terms? Racism and xenophobia are not mutually exclusive from strong social bonding within a community; however, they are not necessarily mutually inclusive either. In future research, if Aldrich can correlate specific incidents of violence to high levels of social capital, he will more clearly link these phenomena. Unlike Aldrich, Comfort and her colleagues focus on a broader conception of resilience, one that stretches past recovery and considers cognition—how decision makers recognize risk, develop strategies for action, and work, often collaboratively, to reduce that risk. Whereas Aldrich’s unit of analysis resides in the aggregate behavior of neighborhoods, Comfort and her colleagues explore how individuals, organizations, and interorganizational networks create a common operating picture to facilitate the shared governance of risk reduction. Resilience represents, in the authors’ view, the effective design, implementation, and continual evaluation and adjustment of disaster-related policies and management practices. There is no one-size-fits-all approach or one set of indicators (or threshold points to interpret those indicators) to ensure the proper management of a distributed system of actors. Unlike routine emergencies (e.g., structure fires, traffic accidents, and so forth), decision makers must often first make sense of a unique set of circumstances and then improvise. Comfort and her colleagues suggest the development and integration of decision support for situations in which information technologies can help decision makers overcome uncertain and stressful conditions. This argument is essentially Louise K. Comfort’s principal contribution to the field. There is much work left to do, however, to effectively model multiple systems, map their interdependences, and accurately anticipate key threshold points that indicate escalating risk. Comfort, Boin, and Demchak’s framework affords researchers opportunities to apply these principles across a variety of cases. Admittedly, the complex interaction between geographic regions, sociotechnical systems, and risk in its many forms defies simple characterization. Both books expand our understanding of the interface between resilience and a number of hazards including earthquakes, tsunamis, hurricanes flooding, avian flu, and terrorism. Their focus on the vulnerability of traditional critical infrastructure to recurrent and recognized hazards, including man-made asymmetric terror threats, however, fails to identify other emerging critical infrastructures upon which society depends. Both books, as well as most if not all of the research in the fields of public administration and political science, unfortunately, fail to anticipate the next battleground or domain that increasingly represents systemic vulnerability to societies around the world—cyberspace. President George H.W. Bush and members of his administration argued against what they labeled as a pre-9/11 mindset of those who opposed policies intended to facilitate the flow and exchange of information throughout the law enforcement and intelligence communities during the war on terrorism. Aside from the virtue and effectiveness of some of those policies, a similar argument can be made today that many policy makers and researchers are operating in a pre-catastrophic, cyber-attack mentality. President Obama, in his 2013 state of the union address as well as other public officials and news agencies around the world have identified the threat of cyber terror, crime, warfare, and technical failure as significant societal risks with many cascades. More researchers should heed the call. Indeed, the fields of public administration and political science should more systemically address the critical vulnerabilities in cyberspace that could lead to systemic failure to an extent we have not fully considered. Although Comfort and her colleagues do not address cyberspace specifically, researchers can incorporate the framework of Comfort et al., working backward to map the interdependencies that exist within and without this critical infrastructure. That type of work would inform policymakers preparing for potential contingencies and cascades. Otherwise, we may remain flatfooted until a massive attack or systemic failure occurs. Both books would be appropriate for masters and doctoral-level courses not just in standard emergency management and homeland security programs but in other fields such as international relations, international development, public administration, public policy, and security studies. These books are relevant also to disciplines that have longer traditions of studying resilience such as engineering and psychology. Comfort and her colleagues take one approach that may be particularly attractive to an instructor either designing a course or looking to augment an existing one. They critique existing orthodoxy in terms of emergency management structure and process and urge practitioners to focus not just on the laws and sets of administrative procedures that shape and constrain government action, but to take a more systemic approach in the designing of disaster management policy that spans scales of action, social sectors, and other sociotechnical systems. Aldrich calls for policies that build and strengthen civic infrastructures such as the capacity of communities to work together and with others to achieve recovery. In an interdependent world of increasingly social and technological complexity, the prevention of all accidents (see Wildavsky 1988 and Perrow 1999), the mitigation of all natural hazards, or the elimination of all asymmetric terror threats is improbable, though desired. Although societies invest significant capital to prevent hazards and protect people from harm, disasters continue to occur. How societies respond to those external shocks—that is, how they protect life and property and maintain continuity of operations in the face of uncertainty and adversity—marks a certain societal strength. Modeling resilience represents a complex task. Resilience is made up of multiple dimensions, all of which require various measures. Each scale has its own set of participants and rules, and often its own unique interface with potential hazards. A key task for researchers is to explore more explicitly these various scales of action and link their interdependencies in order to more accurately identify risk and prepare for potential breakdowns. Comfort and her colleagues and Aldrich offer foundational perspectives. Innovative applications of simulation modeling offer paths to explore vulnerabilities and the interface between complex systems and recurring risk. Scientific advancement in recognizing risk provides opportunities to reduce the surprise associated with hazards and the uncertainty related to managing disasters when they do occur. What Comfort and her colleagues remind us is that the technical data generated by such capabilities go only as far as those who interpret them and develop strategies for collective action that effectively reduce risk. Aldrich and Comfort and colleagues have witnessed extreme events, both personally and professionally, and endeavor to translate their research into practical policy recommendations. Comfort and her colleagues hope to “translate a social technical approach to resilience into action, at a sufficient scale and scope that a change in performance does occur” across jurisdictions (p. 283). There is, however, no quick fix to facilitate more resilient communities. Resilience represents the outcome of policies and practice exhibited over an extended period of time. Both Aldrich and Comfort et al recognize the long-term commitment needed to effect change. Much as Jeffrey Sachs (2005) has advocated the role for clinical economists in promoting international development, acting much like physicians who diagnose and prescribe treatments for their patients, the authors call for a proactive set of practitioners and researchers who, armed with evidence-based research, may empower communities to more effectively recognize and reduce extreme risk. With dedication and luck, the next generation of resilience scholars will further operationalize the tools and strategies outlined by these two very useful books.
